attributes.title: Level 5

subgroups.name: build 1

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use comments to create multiple sections in the editor to better organize your code?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What code might be placed underneath each comment?

❓ How do you create blank lines in the JavaScript editor?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡  Explain to the ninja that typing // tells the project to skip over the text that follows and move onto the next line of code. Just as when naming sprites, it’s useful to be short and descriptive when writing comments. 

💡  Encourage the ninja to use best practices when adding comments to their code. It’s helpful to space out comments in the editor, so that code can be placed in the lines between them. They can use the Enter key to create blank lines between comments. They should also add a space after the slashes in the comment, before adding the text.
steps.instructions:
Begin the project by adding code comments to organize where the code will go in the editor!


Add comments with these descriptions to the project: set up, variable set up, plate sprite code, on A button pressed, on countdown end.


Start each comment with // and create several blank lines between each comment.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you replace mySprite with the name of the plate sprite in sprites.create and setPosition?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Which values might you use as x and y coordinates, so that the plate sprite appears on the bottom center of the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can always toggle back to blocks to use the coordinate grid to select a sprite’s position on screen.
steps.instructions:
Add a plate sprite to place the cookies on top of!


Open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] underneath // plate sprite code. Select the plate sprite from the gallery, then replace mySprite with plate.


Set the plate sprite’s position by opening Sprites and dragging [set (mySprite) position to x y] underneath the code that creates the plate sprite. Update the sprite’s name and the x (0-160)  and y (0-120) parameters so that it appears on the bottom center of the screen.


Click ▶ to see a plate sprite appear on the screen!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you select the cookie image from My Assets as the cookie sprite’s image?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why should the cookie sprite’s code be placed inside the curly brackets { } of the controller events?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that the curly brackets { } used in the controller code act as the container that holds the rest of the code inside of it. Point out to the ninja that the block statements inside the curly brackets are indented. Show the ninja how they can press the Tab key to indent the code, if needed.
steps.instructions:
Code cookies to appear whenever the A button is pressed!


Open Controller and drag [run code on (button) button (event)] underneath // on A button pressed. Use the default property A and default event argument ControllerButtonEvent.Pressed. 


Then, open Sprites and drag [sprite (img) of kind (kind)] inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event. Click on the palette, then select the cookie image from My Assets. Rename the sprite cookie.


Click ▶ to see a cookie appear on the screen whenever the A button is pressed!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you declare a new variable and assign it an initial value?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might a variable be set to assign the cookie sprite’s y-coordinate?

❓ What does the symbol = represent in this line of code? How does it work?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja make the connection between the [set variable to] block in the blocks editor, and using the let keyword in JavaScript. Both actions assign an initial value to the variable and allow the variable to be referenced later in the program.

💡 In JavaScript, a single equal sign = represents an assignment operator. This symbol assigns the variable named on the left to a value typed on the right of the operator.
steps.instructions:
Use a variable to make the cookie sprite appear on top of the plate sprite!


Underneath // variable set up, type let then the name of the cookie sprite with Y at the end of the name. 


Add a space, then type an assignment operator =, which will assign an initial value to the variable. 


Type the y value of the plate sprites after the assignment operator, so that the code reads:


let cookieY = 100

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use the new variable to assign the cookie sprite’s y-coordinate, inside the curly brackets { } of the controller event?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What will the cookie sprite’s y position be set to? How do you know?

❓ Why should the cookie sprite have the same x position as the plate sprite?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that the cookie sprite will be set to the same x and y-coordinates as the plate sprite, in order for the cookies to appear on top of the plates. The cookie’s y-coordinate will be initially set to 100, based on the values of the cookieY variable.
steps.instructions:
Use the new variable to set the cookie sprite’s position!


Open Sprites and drag [set (mySprite) position to x y] underneath the code that creates the cookie sprite, inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event. 


Update the sprite name, then change the  x-coordinate so that the cookie is placed in the same x position as the plate sprite. Then, type the name of the cookieY variable as the y-coordinate. 


Click ▶ to see a cookie placed in the same position as the plate sprite when the A button is pressed!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you decrease the variable that sets the cookie sprite’s y-coordinate by using a subtraction assignment operator  -=  every time the A button is pressed?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens to the y value of the cookie sprite when the A button is pressed? Where will the next cookie sprite appear on the screen?

❓ How does a subtraction assignment operator -= change each cookie sprite’s y value?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja connect the subtraction assignment operator  -= in JavaScript with the [change variable by] block in the blocks editor. Both actions cause the variable to change by a certain value. In this case, the value to the right of the operator -= (2) is subtracted from the initial value of cookieY (100) each time the A button is pressed.

💡 Remind the ninja that in order for a sprite to appear higher on the screen, it needs to have a smaller y value. For this reason, a value should be subtracted from the y variables’ initial value to make the cookie appear higher on the screen, “stacked” on top of the previous cookie.
steps.instructions:
Oh no—when the A button is pressed, only 1 cookie is visible on the plate! Code the cookie sprites to appear stacked on top of each other.


Create a blank line underneath the code that sets the cookie sprite’s position, inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event. 


Type the name of the cookieY variable followed by a space, then use a subtraction assignment operator  -= to decrease the sprite’s y position by 2 each time the A button is pressed. 


Now, each time the A button is pressed, the sprite’s y-coordinate will be decreased by 2, and it will appear stacked on top of the previous cookie.


Click ▶ then press A to see each new cookie appear stacked on top of the previous one!

steps.hints: ❓Did you declare a new variable to track how many cookie sprites are created, and assign an initial value?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why might it be useful to use a variable to count how many cookie sprites appear on the screen?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that variables are very useful for storing and using data to impact events in a project. This data will be used later in the project to inform the user how many total cookie sprites were stacked.
steps.instructions:
Keep track of how many cookie sprites are stacked on the plate! 


Create a new blank line under // variable set up. 


Declare a new variable by typing the keyword let, then the cookie sprite’s name, followed by Stack. Add a space, then type an assignment operator = and assign the variable a value of 0, so that the code reads:


let cookieStack = 0.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use an addition assignment operator to increase the cookieStack variable when the A button is pressed?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens to the values of cookieStack when the A button is pressed?

❓ What does the += symbol represent? How does it work?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja connect the addition assignment operator  += in JavaScript with the [change variable by] block in the blocks editor. Both actions cause the variable to change by a certain value. In this case, the value to the right of the += (1) is added to the initial value of cookieStack (0), each time the A button is pressed.

💡 Help the ninja connect the use of the variable to count how many cookie sprites appear on the screen. Each time the A button is pressed, 1 will be added to the cookieStack variable. Reiterate to the ninja that variables are useful because they can be called and updated throughout the program to store certain data.
steps.instructions:
Whenever a new cookie sprite appears, increase the value of the stack variable by 1. 


Create a blank line underneath the existing code inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event.


Type the name of the variable that counts the cookie stack, a space, followed by an addition assignment operator += and a value of 1, so that the code reads:


cookieStack += 1


The addition assignment operator will add the value on the right to the variable’s existing value, then assign the variable the updated value. 


Now, the project will count how many cookie sprites appear on the plate.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you set the Boolean canStack variable as true when the project starts, and false when the countdown ends?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What is similar and different about assigning a variable a Boolean value in JavaScript compared to blocks?

❓ What will happen when the countdown ends?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Help the ninja recall dragging <true> or <false> Booleans into [set variable to] blocks in the blocks editor. Variables are assigned in the same way in JavaScript; the only difference being having to type out true or false instead of dragging it into the code.

💡 Remind the ninja that variables can help control certain events in a project. In this example, code is added to the project so that the user is able to stack cookies when the project begins, but is no longer able to do so once the countdown ends.
steps.instructions:
Add a countdown timer, then set when the user can and cannot add new cookies!


Create a new variable underneath // variable set up. Type the keyword let, then use canStack as the variable name. Add an assignment operator = and assign a Boolean true as the variable’s value so that the code reads:


let canStack = true


This will allow the user to stack cookies when the project has started. 


Open Info and drag [start countdown (10) (s)] below the code that declares the canStack variable. Update the parameter so that the user only has a short amount of time to stack cookies.


Prevent the user from stacking cookies when the countdown ends by opening Info and dragging [run code on countdown end] under // on countdown end. Create a blank line inside the curly brackets { } of the onCountdownEnd event and type the canStack variable name, followed by an assignment operator = and a  Boolean false, so that the code looks like:


canStack = false

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use an equality operator inside the parentheses of the if condition to check if the canStack variable’s value equals true?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Why is it necessary to add a conditional to the cookie sprite’s code to only run when canStack == true?

❓ What does the symbol == represent in JavaScript? How does it work?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that a conditional is needed in the cookie sprite’s code to make sure that cookies are only able to be stacked while canStack equals true. This ensures that cookies will not be able to be stacked when the countdown ends, and canStack is set to false.

💡 In JavaScript, the symbol  == represents an equality operator. This symbol checks to see if the value typed on the left of the operator is equal to the value on the right. If the value of canStack is equal to true when the A button is pressed, then the if condition’s code will run.

💡 Help the ninja make the connection between the equality operator and the comparison blocks in the blocks editor. Both actions are able to check for equal values on either side of the symbol to determine what code to run.
steps.instructions:
Allow cookie sprites to be stacked only when canStack is true. 


Open Logic and drag if  underneath // on A button pressed inside the curly brackets { } of the controller.A event. Inside the parentheses of the if condition, type the canStack variable name followed by an equality operator == so the code reads:


canStack == true


In JavaScript, equality operators are used to check if the variable’s value on the left of the operator is equal to the value on the right. 


Cut (Ctrl + X) and paste (Ctrl + V) the cookie sprite’s code inside the curly brackets { } of the if conditional.


Click ▶ to notice that cookie sprites can only be stacked while the countdown is running.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add a pause and a sound effect once the countdown ends?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ How do you use the dot operator . to access the list of possible sound effects?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can delete .baDing, then retype the dot operator . to access the list of possible sound effects.
steps.instructions:
Add a time delay and a sound effect when the countdown ends!


Open Loops and drag [pause (100) ms] onto a blank line inside the curly brackets { } of the onCountdownEnd event. Update the parameter so the project pauses briefly when the countdown ends.


Add a sound effect to the time delay by opening Music, dragging out [play (toPlay) (playbackMode)] underneath the pause code. Use the dot operator . to select a sound to play from the code completion tool.


Click ▶ to see the project pause, then play a sound when the countdown timer ends!

steps.hints: ❓Did you use an assignment operator = to save the user provided value to the playerGuess variable?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ Did you place strings in quotation marks, use plus signs + to join, or concatenate, variables, and space words out correctly?

❓ How are the cookieStack variables used to tell the user how many cookies were stacked in the project?

 

Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that concatenation means joining multiple strings and/or variables in order.

💡 Point out to the ninja that this dialog box should share how many cookies were stacked on each plate by the end of the project. The ninja should play the project, read the message, and make sure that each string and variable is placed correctly to communicate this information.

💡 Prompt the ninja to notice that the variable names used in the code turn into their values when the dialog box appears. This is a useful way to share stored data back to the user in a project.
steps.instructions:
Once the countdown ends, ask the user to guess how many cookies they think they stacked.


Declare a new variable underneath inside the curly brackets { } of the onCountdownEnd event, above the music code by typing the keyword let. 


Use playerGuess as the variable name, then type an assignment operator =. Open Game and drag [ask for number (message)] to the right of the assignment operator. Notice how the code block turns into JavaScript text:


game.askForNumber(null)


The askForNumber function takes two parameters: message and answerLength. The message parameter takes a string argument and answerLength takes a number argument, which sets the maximum number of digits that the user can enter. 


Replace null with  a string surrounded by quotation marks that asks the user how many cookies they think they stacked. Add a comma , then use 2 as the answerLength argument.


Click ▶ to see the project prompt the user to guess how many cookies they stacked!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use an inequality operator != to check if playerGuess is not equal to the cookieStack ?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What needs to be true, in order for the else if condition’s code run? 

❓ What does the symbol != represent in JavaScript? How does it work?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 In JavaScript, an exclamation point and an equal sign != represent an inequality operator. This symbol checks to see if the value typed on the left of the operator is not equal to the value on the right. If the value of playerGuess is equal to cookieStack when the countdown ends, then the if condition’s code will run. Else if the value of playerGuess is not equal to cookieStack when the countdown ends, then the else if condition’s code will run.

💡Help the ninja make the connection between the inequality operator and the comparison blocks in the blocks editor. In the blocks editor, there was an option to select the != symbol from the code completion tool of the comparison block. Both actions are able to check for unequal values on either side of the symbol.
steps.instructions:
Check whether the user’s guess matches the number of cookies they actually stacked!


Open Logic and drag [if/else] under // on countdown end inside the curly brackets { } of the onCountdownEnd event. Inside the parentheses of the if condition, replace true with playerGuess. Add an equality operator ==, followed by cookieStack. The if condition’s code will run if the player’s guess is equal to the number of cookies actually stacked.


Change the else condition into an else if by typing if followed by a set of parentheses, so that the code looks like:


else if () {} 


Copy (Ctrl + C) the code inside the parentheses of the if condition, then paste (Ctrl + V) the code inside the parentheses of the else if condition. Change the equality operator ==  to an inequality operator != by typing an exclamation point and an equal sign. Now, the else if condition’s code will run if the player’s guess is not equal to the number of cookies actually stacked.

steps.hints: ❓ Did you use a plus sign (+) to concatenate, or join, the string and the variable so that a sentence is displayed?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓Did you use quotation marks to separate the strings from the variables in showLongText? 

❓ Which message will appear when playerGuess is not equal to cookieStack?

❓ Does each dialog box’s message appear correctly when the project is played?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Point out to the ninja that when they are concatenating multiple strings and variables, they need to make sure that symbols and spaces are placed correctly. All strings need to be contained by quotation marks, and plus signs + need to be added to separate strings from variables and join them together. Encourage the ninja to test out their project to see how the dialog boxes appear and revise the syntax as needed.

💡 Walk the ninja through the logic of the code. If the player’s guess is equal to the actual cookie stack total, then a message will display that tells the user that their guess was correct, and the total number of cookies. If the player’s guess is not equal to the actual cookie stack total, then a message will display telling the user what their guess was and what the actual total number of cookies was.
steps.instructions:
Add dialog boxes to tell the user how their guess compared to the actual number of cookies stacked!


Open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] inside the curly brackets { } of the if condition. Replace null with a string in quotes that tells the user that their guess was correct. After the string, concatenate a variable’s value by typing + then cookieStack.


After the variable name, type + again, then another string that says “ cookies were stacked!”


This message will show only if the user’s guess matches the actual number of cookies stacked.


Copy (Ctrl + C) the showLongText code and paste (Ctrl + V) it inside the curly brackets { } of the else if condition. Edit the strings so that the message also uses the playerGuess variable to tell how many cookies the user expected to stack, and the cookieStack variable to tell how many cookies were actually stacked. 


This message will show if the user’s guess does not match the actual number of cookies stacked. Be sure to check  that strings, variables, and symbols are placed correctly when the message appears! 


Click ▶ to see whether the user input matches the actual number of cookies stacked in the project!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you type a number between 1-15 to set the color parameter in the parentheses in scene.setBackgroundColor(color)?
steps.senseiHelp:
Ask the ninja:

❓ What background color might you use as a backdrop for the project?

❓ What directions might tell the user how to play the game?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Remind the ninja that they can always click on the palette for one of the images in the code to open the editor. Once opened, they can hover their cursor over each individual color to find the corresponding value to use as a background color.

💡 Remind the ninja that strings need to be placed inside of quotation marks and that parameters need to be separated by a comma, otherwise the code will not be able to run correctly.
steps.instructions:
Finish the project by adding a background color and directions!


Open Scene, drag out [set background color to (color)] into the editor underneath //set up. Click between the parentheses to set a color parameter using a number 1-15.


Open Game and drag [show long text (str) (layout)] onto a blank line underneath the code to set the background color. Update the string and layout parameters, so that the dialog box shares directions for the user to follow.


Click ▶ to see the completed project!

subgroups.title: Cookie Stacker
subgroups.introduction: Create a project in JavaScript that uses assignment, equality, and math operators to create and change variables, in order to calculate the number of cookies stacked on the screen.

validationItems.text: Create 1 plate sprite and set its position.
Use a controller button pressed event to create cookie sprites.
Declare a variable to store the changing  y values, use them in a setPosition function, and decrease its value on every button press.
Declare a variable with an initial value of 0 and increment its value by 1 on every button press.
Declare a Boolean variable and initialize it to true.
Use the startCountdown and onCountdownEnd functions. When the countdown ends, set the Boolean variable to false.
Use the Boolean variable to let the player stack only when it is true.
Add a pause and a music effect.
Use the askForNumber function and store the user’s input as a variable.
Use an if / else if statement to check to see if the player’s guess is equal to or not equal to their guess.
Use the showLongText function to tell the player how many cookies were stacked and if their guess was correct. Use the + sign to concatenate the message and the variable.
Add a background color and instructions using the showLongText function.

attributes.description: You’ve reached Level 5 of Blue Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about assignment and equality operators, which can be used to assign, change, and check for a variable’s value. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 5:

badges.title: One Equals Sign or Two?
badges.description: Use the correct symbols to create assignment and equality operators to assign, change, and check for a variable’s value in JavaScript.

badges.title: Let There Be Variables
badges.description: Create a variable using let in JavaScript.

badges.title: Concatenation Station
badges.description: Concatenate two or more strings together using the + operator.

badges.title: Asset Depreciation
badges.description: Use the subtraction assignment operator to decrease the value of a number variable.

badges.title: Incremental Growth
badges.description: Use the addition assignment operator to increase the value of a number variable.

badges.title: I’m Thinking of a Number
badges.description: Use the askForNumber function to assign a user-inputted value to a variable.

badges.title: It’s Back on the Menu
badges.description: Write code that runs when the Menu button is pressed.
